results.result: The authors developed HIV-AFMACS, a reporter virus displaying a streptavidin-binding affinity tag (SBP-ΔLNGFR) at the surface of infected cells, enabling one-step magnetic selection with streptavidin beads and biotin-mediated release. The system routinely achieved ≥90% purity from mixed populations containing 20-40% infected cells, with ≤10% loss in flow-through.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C15-C20 collectively demonstrate successful development and validation of the HIV-AFMACS system. The molecular design is clearly described (C15-C18), and experimental validation shows high selection efficiency in both cell lines and primary T cells (C19-C20). Flow cytometry data in Figure 1 provides strong quantitative evidence for the claimed purities.

results.result: The authors generated a high-coverage proteomic atlas of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells, quantitating approximately 9000 proteins across multiple donors with 650 HIV-dependent changes (q<0.05). Over 90% of proteins were quantitated using two or more unique peptides, and T cell activation alone caused extensive remodeling with 29% of proteins changing >2-fold.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C21, C88, C94 are well-supported by comprehensive proteomic data deposited in ProteomeXchange (C112). The depth of coverage (9000 proteins) and quality metrics (>90% with ≥2 peptides) exceed previous studies (C90-C93), and statistical analysis with FDR correction is appropriate. The claim of being the 'first high coverage' atlas is justified by comparison with prior work.

results.result: The authors confirmed depletion of known HIV accessory protein targets in primary T cells, including Vpu substrates (tetherin, CD4, SNAT1), Nef substrates (CD4, SERINC5), Vif substrates (APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 families), and Vpr substrates (UNG, HLTF, ZGPAT, VPRBP, MUS81, EME1, MCM10, TET2). APOBEC3B, SERINC1, and HLA-C were not depleted, while HLA-A and HLA-B were depleted, consistent with NL4-3 HIV variants.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C44 validate known accessory protein targets with proteomic data (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and are supported by extensive prior literature. The temporal dynamics (C22, C24) and selective depletion patterns (C40-C43) provide additional validation. The consistency with established mechanisms strengthens confidence in the overall dataset quality.

results.result: Seven viral open reading frames were identified in the proteomic analysis. Viral regulatory and accessory proteins from fully spliced transcripts (Tat, Rev, Nef-P2A, SBP-ΔLNGFR) were expressed early and peaked at 24 hr, while structural proteins from unspliced transcripts (Gag, Gagpol) were expressed late and increased progressively from 24 to 48 hr.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by temporal proteomic data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and consistent with established HIV transcription patterns (C46 cites Karn and Stoltzfus, 2012). The differential timing of early vs. late viral proteins validates the experimental system and provides internal consistency checks.

results.result: Known accessory protein-dependent changes characterized in T cell lines account for 46% (297/650) of proteins regulated by HIV in primary T cells, including 59% (175/299) of downregulated proteins. The authors infer that accessory proteins account for much of the proteomic remodeling, and that downregulated proteins correlate better with T cell line data than upregulated proteins, possibly because upregulated proteins reflect indirect, cell-type-specific transcriptional changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are supported by quantitative analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B). The inferences in C101-C104 are reasonable given the data showing strong correlation for downregulated proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) and the mechanistic understanding that direct accessory protein targets are depleted. However, the speculation about upregulated proteins (C104) is less directly supported.

results.result: HIV infection causes marked increases in proteins associated with lipid and sterol metabolism. Similar effects have been reported in T cell lines at the transcriptional level and attributed to Nef expression, and several proteins in these pathways are indirectly regulated by Vpr.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are supported by proteomic data (Figure 4B-C) and consistent with prior transcriptional studies (C53 cites Shrivastava et al., 2016; van 't Wout et al., 2005). The Vpr connection (C54) is supported by reference to Greenwood et al., 2019 and data in Figure 4C showing overlap with Vpr-regulated proteins.

results.result: 192 proteins not identified and/or regulated in T cell lines were found to be regulated by HIV in primary T cells, including ARID5A and PTPN22. These proteins were consistently depleted across all donors with fold change >2 and were identified with 9-14 unique peptides. Proteins unique to primary T cells were significantly more likely to be regulated by HIV (10.5% vs 6.9%, p<0.0001).
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10, C55, C60-C61, C89 are supported by comparative proteomic analysis and validated by immunoblot (Figure 3D-E). The statistical significance (C89) is appropriately calculated using Fisher's exact test. The identification of primary cell-specific targets represents a key advantage of the system over cell line models.

results.result: Control experiments using lentivectors expressing SBP-ΔLNGFR alone or with Tat showed minimal effects, with only 37/8518 (0.4%) proteins significantly perturbed and only 1/576 HIV-regulated proteins (MYB) also regulated by controls. The authors conclude it is very unlikely that the selection system or VSVg pseudotyping caused significant artifactual changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59, C97 are supported by comprehensive control experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). The minimal overlap between HIV effects and control lentivector effects (C59) provides strong evidence against systematic artifacts. The inference in C97 is well-justified by the quantitative data showing only 1/650 overlapping changes.

results.result: Substrates of different HIV accessory proteins can be distinguished by characteristic temporal regulation patterns. Vpr substrates showed near-maximal depletion by 24 hr in infected cells with partial depletion in uninfected cells (due to virion-packaged Vpr), while Vif, Nef, and Vpu substrates increased progressively from 24-48 hr only in infected cells. Based on temporal profiles, ARID5A and PTPN22 are likely novel Vpr substrates specific for primary T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C68 are supported by temporal proteomic data (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and consistent with known biology of Vpr packaging (C63-C64). The inference that ARID5A and PTPN22 are Vpr substrates (C67) is reasonable based on temporal clustering, though direct mechanistic validation would strengthen this conclusion. The connection to ARID5B (C68) provides supporting evidence.

results.result: The authors identified DPH7 and FMR1 as novel Vif-dependent targets. Both proteins were depleted in primary CD4+ T cells and CEM-T4s infected with WT but not ΔVif viruses, showed more profound depletion than PP2A-related proteins, and depletion was confirmed by immunoblot in both viral infection and Vif transgene experiments. Together with APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 families, these account for all significant Vif-dependent changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C69-C70, C78-C84 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: proteomic data comparing WT vs ΔVif (Figure 5A-B, 5E), immunoblot validation (Figure 5F-G), and Vif transgene sufficiency experiments (Figure 5G). The necessity and sufficiency experiments (C83) provide strong mechanistic evidence. The claim that these account for all Vif-dependent changes (C84) is supported by comprehensive analysis.

results.result: Vif-dependent depletion of PPP2R5 family proteins causes increased AURKB T232 phosphorylation. AURKB activity is enhanced by T232 auto-phosphorylation and antagonized by PP2A-B56. Increased AURKB phosphorylation was observed in CEM-T4s transduced with Vif and in AFMACS-selected primary T cells infected with WT HIV, serving as a functional correlate of PPP2R5D depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 are supported by immunoblot data (Figure 5C-D) and established biochemistry (C72-C73). The functional readout of AURKB phosphorylation provides mechanistic validation of PPP2R5 depletion and demonstrates downstream consequences. This represents a well-validated signaling pathway affected by Vif.

results.result: 33 newly described Vpr substrates from a recent study (Greenwood et al., 2019) were quantitated in primary T cells and 32 decreased in abundance. This recent work showed that most protein-level changes in HIV-infected CEM-T4s may be explained by primary and secondary effects of Vpr, including degradation of at least 34 additional substrates beyond canonical targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114, C49 are supported by data in Figure 3C and citations to Greenwood et al., 2016 and 2019. The recapitulation of Vpr effects from cell lines in primary T cells (32/33 substrates decreased) validates both the current system and prior findings. This demonstrates the robustness of Vpr-mediated protein degradation across cell types.

results.result: The authors provide background on differences between primary T cells and T cell lines: CEM-T4 is highly permissive for HIV; accessory proteins Vif, Nef, and Vpu are required in primary T cells but not many cell lines; HIV is restricted by type I IFN in primary but not CEM-derived T cells; cancer cell line utility is limited by retention of primary cell characteristics; and inter-individual variability affects T cell activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14, C48 are well-supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide important context for why primary T cell studies are needed and justify the experimental approach. The claims accurately represent prior knowledge in the field.

results.result: The authors argue that AFMACS offers advantages over conventional methods: bead-based magnetic sorting is faster, simpler, and more scalable than FACS; conventional antibody-based selection risks altering cell behavior through receptor cross-linking or bead internalization; AFMACS is antibody-free with biotin-mediated release.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 are supported by appropriate citations (Plouffe et al., 2015; Bernard et al., 2002; Stanciu et al., 1996; Matheson et al., 2014) and demonstrated experimentally. The advantages are well-established in the literature and validated by the successful application in this study achieving high purity and cell viability.

results.result: Previous temporal proteomic analyses of HIV-infected primary T cells had limited coverage (<2000 proteins) and did not detect accessory protein targets. A recent study (Kuo et al., 2018) quantitated 7761 proteins at 96 hr post-infection but 413/650 (64%) of HIV-dependent changes identified in the current study were obscured, including depletion of ARID5A, PTPN22, DPH7, and 19/51 known accessory protein substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93 are supported by appropriate citations and comparative analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 5). The quantitative comparison showing 64% of changes were obscured in the prior study validates the superior sensitivity of the current approach. This justifies the claim of providing a more comprehensive atlas.

results.result: The authors discuss limitations of VSVg pseudotyping: it redirects viral entry to endocytic pathways and may abrogate Env-dependent signaling. However, they argue it is unlikely to cause false positives (only 1/650 changes overlapped with controls) but may cause false negatives by missing Env-CD4/co-receptor interaction effects, which may vary by viral tropism.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 appropriately acknowledge limitations with supporting citations (Aiken, 1997; Arthos et al., 2008; Wu and Yoder, 2009; Wiredja et al., 2018). The inference about false positives (C97) is well-supported by control data (C59). The speculation about false negatives (C98-C99) is reasonable and appropriately cautious, representing good scientific practice in discussing limitations.

results.result: The authors argue that temporal profiling is well-suited for identifying direct viral protein targets, and that accessory proteins account for most proteomic remodeling. Vif was thought to exclusively target APOBEC3 proteins until recently. The novel targets identified (FMR1, ARID5A, PTPN22, DPH7) impact processes relevant for HIV replication including viral infectivity, inflammatory signaling, T cell activation, and translational fidelity.
results.evaluation: Claims C100, C105-C109 are supported by the data and appropriate citations. The functional relevance of novel targets (C106-C109) is established by prior literature, though direct demonstration of their roles in HIV replication in the current system would strengthen these claims. The overall argument about the value of temporal profiling (C100) is validated by the successful identification of novel targets.

results.result: The HIV-AFMACS sequence is available from GenBank (MK435310), the proviral construct will be distributed via NIH AIDS Reagent Program, and all mass spectrometry data have been deposited to ProteomeXchange (PXD012263).
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C112 are explicitly stated with accession numbers and represent appropriate data and reagent sharing practices. These are verifiable statements about resource availability.

results.result: The HIV-AFMACS system is a novel technical tool that uses a streptavidin-binding affinity tag (SBP-ΔLNGFR) displayed on infected cells to enable one-step magnetic bead selection, achieving ≥90% purity of HIV-infected primary CD4+ T cells from mixed populations.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly praised the technical innovation. Reviewer 2 states the paper's strengths include 'the technical innovation' and Reviewer 3 calls the study 'compelling, appropriately controlled.' The editors note reviewers were 'impressed with the magnitude of your data set' and the technical approach, leading to acceptance as a Tools and Resources paper.

results.result: The study quantitated approximately 9000 proteins across multiple donors and identified 650 HIV-dependent protein changes (q<0.05), representing the first high-coverage proteomic atlas of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells with >90% of proteins quantitated using two or more unique peptides.
results.evaluation: Reviewers unanimously praised the dataset quality and scope. Reviewer 1 notes 'This is the largest data set in using primary CD4+ T cells to-date' and calls it 'technically sound.' Reviewer 2 highlights 'the depth and stringency of the mass spec data obtained' as a key strength. The editors emphasize reviewers were 'impressed with the magnitude of your data set.'

results.result: Control experiments demonstrate that SBP-ΔLNGFR expression and lentivector transduction cause minimal proteomic perturbations, with only 37/8518 (0.4%) proteins significantly affected and only 1/576 HIV-regulated proteins also regulated by control vectors.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly raises concern about this control, stating 'the authors did not include an evaluation of whether the expression of SBP-LNGFR and its display on the cell surface causes any changes in expression of cellular proteins, as an important negative control.' While the manuscript presents control data, the reviewer questions whether 'the potential effects of LNGFR overexpression and bead binding can truly be disregarded,' indicating the controls may be insufficient.

results.result: 192 proteins not identified/regulated in T cell lines were found regulated by HIV in primary T cells, including ARID5A and PTPN22, which are consistently depleted across all donors (fold change >2) and likely represent novel Vpr substrates based on temporal regulation patterns.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these findings but express concerns about functional validation. Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'focus on novel cellular factors (ARID5A, PTPN22, DPH7, and FMR1) but the functional significance of these interactions is unclear.' Reviewer 2 states 'there is rather limited validation of new or interesting hits.' However, the data identifying these proteins as primary cell-specific and Vpr-dependent is not disputed.

results.result: DPH7 and FMR1 are novel Vif-dependent targets showing profound depletion in WT vs ΔVif infected cells in both primary T cells and CEM-T4s, with Vif being both necessary and sufficient for their depletion as confirmed by immunoblot validation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these novel Vif targets but question their functional significance. Reviewer 1 states 'the functional significance of these interactions is unclear' and Reviewer 2 notes 'there is rather limited validation of new or interesting hits and no characterization of why they (in particular the highlighted factors DPH7 and FMR1) are affected by HIV or the roles they might play.' The identification is accepted but functional characterization is deemed insufficient.

results.result: The study confirms depletion of known accessory protein targets in primary T cells, including Vpu targets (tetherin, CD4, SNAT1), Nef targets (CD4, SERINC5), Vif targets (APOBEC3, PPP2R5 families), and Vpr targets (UNG, HLTF, ZGPAT, VPRBP, MUS81, EME1, MCM10, TET2), with characteristic temporal patterns distinguishing different accessory protein substrates.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these confirmatory findings. Reviewer 1 notes 'over half of the 600+ changes were dependent on Vpr and Vif/Nef/Vpu' and calls the study 'technically sound.' These known targets serve as positive controls validating the approach, though reviewers emphasize the limited novelty, with Reviewer 1 noting 'my main concern is novelty and overlap with prior and parallel work.'

results.result: Known accessory protein-dependent changes characterized in T cell lines account for 46% (297/650) of proteins regulated by HIV in primary T cells, including 59% of proteins decreased in abundance, suggesting accessory proteins account for much of the proteomic remodeling.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this comparative analysis. Reviewer 1 notes 'The authors indicate 40-60% Venn overlap with proteomic studies in CEM cells' without disputing the finding. This quantitative comparison between primary cells and cell lines is treated as a valid contribution to understanding the extent of conservation across cell types.

results.result: HIV infection causes marked increases in proteins associated with lipid and sterol metabolism in primary T cells, with several proteins in these pathways indirectly regulated by Vpr, consistent with previous transcriptional studies in T cell lines.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these pathway-level findings. The observation is presented as confirmatory of previous work at the transcriptional level, now extended to the protein level in primary cells. No reviewer raises concerns about the lipid metabolism findings.

results.result: T cell activation causes extensive proteomic remodeling (29% of proteins changing >2 fold), and seven viral ORFs were identified with temporal expression patterns consistent with HIV transcriptional regulation (early expression of Tat, Rev, Nef-P2A, SBP-ΔLNGFR; late expression of Gag, Gagpol).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not dispute these findings about T cell activation and viral protein expression kinetics. Reviewer 3 asks the authors to 'comment on the impact of T cell activation of HIV permissivity' and whether their data 'can be used to illuminate the changes that occur on TCR cross linking that drive permissivity,' indicating interest in leveraging rather than challenging these observations.

results.result: 1252 (14%) cellular proteins quantitated in primary T cells were not identified in CEM-T4s, and proteins unique to primary T cells were significantly more likely to be regulated by HIV (10.5% vs 6.9%, p<0.0001). Additionally, 413/650 (64%) HIV-dependent changes were obscured in a recent comparable study.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the comparative analysis showing differences between primary cells and cell lines. Reviewer 1 acknowledges 'The authors indicate 40-60% Venn overlap with proteomic studies in CEM cells' and the focus on primary cell-specific factors. The statistical comparison demonstrating enrichment of HIV regulation among primary cell-specific proteins is not challenged.

results.result: VSVg pseudotyping redirects viral entry to an endocytic pathway and may abrogate Env-dependent signaling, though control experiments suggest VSVg caused minimal artefactual changes. However, the absence of Env-CD4/co-receptor interactions may result in underestimation of proteomic changes induced by full-length HIV.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly criticizes this limitation, stating 'it is unfortunate that ΔEnv viruses were chosen for the analysis considering the large impact Env-CD4/CoR binding can have on primary T cell responses' and notes 'it seems reasonable that their viruses could have been pseudotyped with wild-type Envelope proteins instead of VSV-G.' The reviewer requests 'Further discussion of this issue would be warranted,' indicating the VSVg approach is a significant concern affecting interpretation.

results.result: PPP2R5D depletion and increased AURKB T232 phosphorylation are observed in AFMACS-selected primary T cells infected with WT HIV, consistent with previous findings in CEM-T4s showing Vif-dependent PP2A-B56 depletion causes increased aurora kinase substrate phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these confirmatory findings extending previous CEM-T4 observations to primary cells. The AURKB phosphorylation serves as a functional readout validating the PPP2R5 depletion, and no concerns are raised about this mechanistic validation.

results.result: APOBEC3B and SERINC1 were not depleted by HIV in primary T cells, while HLA-A and HLA-B (but not HLA-C) were depleted, consistent with known Nef/Vpu variant specificities from NL4-3 HIV.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not dispute these negative and selective depletion findings. These observations serve as important specificity controls demonstrating that not all family members are targeted and that the system recapitulates known allele-specific effects.

results.result: The HIV-AFMACS sequence is deposited in GenBank (MK435310), the proviral construct will be distributed via NIH AIDS Reagent Program, and all mass spectrometry data are deposited in ProteomeXchange (PXD012263).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically praises 'the interactive spreadsheet that provides an easy-to-access and expansive resource.' Reviewer 3 requests the GenBank submission (point 5), which the manuscript indicates was done. The data sharing and resource availability are viewed positively as enabling future research.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the HIV-AFMACS technical innovation (C1-C3, C15-C20) and AFMACS advantages (C85-C87) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval focuses on molecular design and validation data, while peer reviewers emphasize the technical innovation as a key strength leading to acceptance as Tools and Resources paper.

Both evaluate the proteomic dataset quality and coverage (C4-C5, C88, C94) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes depth metrics and comparison to prior studies (C90-C93), while peer reviewers praise 'the magnitude of your data set' and 'depth and stringency of the mass spec data.' Both agree this is the largest primary CD4+ T cell dataset.

Both address control experiments (C56-C59) but with different evaluations. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, emphasizing minimal overlap validates lack of artifacts. Peer Reviewer 2 rates as UNCERTAIN, explicitly questioning whether LNGFR overexpression controls are sufficient and whether 'potential effects can truly be disregarded.'

Both evaluate novel Vif targets (C6-C7, C69-C70, C78-C84) as SUPPORTED for identification but differ in emphasis. OpenEval highlights necessity/sufficiency experiments as strong mechanistic evidence. Peer reviewers accept the identification but criticize 'rather limited validation' and unclear 'functional significance,' particularly for DPH7 and FMR1.

Both address primary cell-specific targets (C8-C10, C60-C61) and novel Vpr substrate ARID5A (C67) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes statistical validation and immunoblot confirmation. Peer reviewers acknowledge findings but express concerns about 'unclear' functional significance of novel factors like ARID5A and PTPN22.

Both evaluate known accessory protein targets (C22-C39) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes these validate dataset quality through consistency with literature. Peer reviewers accept these confirmatory findings as technically sound positive controls but note limited novelty, with Reviewer 1 citing 'concern is novelty and overlap with prior work.'

Both evaluate comparative analysis between primary cells and cell lines (C50-C51, C101-C102) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes strong correlation for downregulated proteins. Peer reviewers accept the 40-60% Venn overlap finding without dispute as valid contribution to understanding conservation across cell types.

Both evaluate lipid metabolism pathway findings (C52-C54) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes consistency with prior transcriptional studies and Vpr connection. Peer reviewers do not challenge these pathway-level findings, treating them as confirmatory extension to protein level in primary cells.

Both evaluate viral protein expression kinetics (C45-C47) and T cell activation effects (C21) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes temporal data consistency with HIV transcription patterns. Peer reviewers accept findings and show interest in leveraging observations, with Reviewer 3 asking to 'comment on impact of T cell activation.'

Both address experimental limitations (C95-C99) but with different evaluations. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, viewing limitations as appropriately acknowledged. Peer Reviewer 2 rates as UNCERTAIN, explicitly criticizing the ΔEnv/VSVg choice as 'unfortunate' given 'large impact Env-CD4/CoR binding can have,' requesting further discussion.

Both evaluate PPP2R5 depletion and AURKB phosphorylation findings (C71-C76) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes functional readout as mechanistic validation. Peer reviewers accept these confirmatory findings extending CEM-T4 observations to primary cells without raising concerns.

Both evaluate data/reagent sharing (C110-C112) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes verifiable accession numbers and appropriate practices. Peer reviewers praise 'interactive spreadsheet' as 'easy-to-access and expansive resource' enabling future research.

Both address AFMACS technical advantages (C85-C87) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval cites literature support and successful application achieving high purity. Peer reviewers incorporate these advantages into overall praise of technical innovation, with all three reviewers highlighting the approach.

Both address comparison with prior studies (C90-C93) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative comparison showing 64% of changes were obscured in prior work, justifying superior sensitivity. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the dataset's magnitude and depth.

Both address primary cell vs cell line differences (C93) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval includes this in comparative analysis of prior studies. Peer reviewers accept statistical enrichment of HIV regulation among primary cell-specific proteins without challenge.

Both evaluate selective depletion patterns (C40-C43) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes these provide validation through specificity. Peer reviewers accept these as important specificity controls demonstrating allele-specific effects and that not all family members are targeted.

Both address Vpr temporal dynamics and packaging (C62-C68, with overlap on C65-C66) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes temporal clustering supporting ARID5A/PTPN22 as Vpr substrates. Peer reviewers accept confirmatory Vpr findings without challenge, though note limited novelty.

OpenEval evaluates recapitulation of Vpr effects from cell lines in primary T cells (C113-C114, C49) as SUPPORTED, demonstrating 32/33 substrates decreased. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though peer reviewers generally accept Vpr confirmatory findings.

OpenEval evaluates contextual claims about why primary T cell studies are needed (C11-C14, C48) as SUPPORTED with appropriate literature citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; these background claims are not specifically addressed by reviewers.

OpenEval evaluates functional relevance of novel targets and value of temporal profiling (C100, C105-C109) as SUPPORTED based on literature citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer reviewers generally request more functional validation of novel hits.
